analysis.one_liner: Requires off-exchange energy trading platforms to register with regulators and curb excessive speculation in oil and gas markets.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 15 bipartisan cosponsors in November 2007, the bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: In the late 1990s and 2000, changes to commodity law left certain electronic energy trading platforms outside the oversight of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the 'Enron loophole.' This bill would have required those platforms to register with the CFTC, imposed position limits to prevent manipulation and excessive speculation, required daily publication of prices and volumes, extended anti-fraud rules, and required reporting of US energy trades placed through foreign exchanges.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who pay gasoline, heating oil, diesel, natural gas, and electricity prices, since the bill aimed to reduce manipulation and speculation that can inflate those prices. Traders and hedgers operating under transparent, level rules also benefit from a market less prone to distortion.

how_it_helps.text: It removes the exemption that let electronic energy trading facilities operate without CFTC oversight, making it unlawful to trade future delivery of energy commodities on an unregistered energy trading facility [S2][S3].

It directs the CFTC to set position limits and accountability levels on energy contracts that prevent price manipulation, excessive speculation, and price distortion, and to force traders who exceed them to reduce or liquidate positions [S2][S3].
Registered facilities must publish daily settlement prices, volume, and open interest, and keep records for five years available to the CFTC and the Department of Justice [S3].
It broadens the prohibition on cheating and defrauding in commodity sales from exchange members to any person, closing a gap in anti-fraud enforcement [S2][S3].
It requires CFTC reporting of US-referenced energy contracts executed on foreign boards of trade through domestic terminals, closing an offshore escape valve [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large energy speculators, hedge funds, and investment banks trading unregulated off-exchange energy swaps would bear compliance costs, position limits, and disclosure requirements. Some traders argued added oversight could reduce market liquidity, and disputed how much speculation actually moved energy prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs: the bill imposes registration, surveillance, daily publication, recordkeeping, and reporting duties on trading facilities and traders, which smaller market participants would bear disproportionately [S3].

Economists genuinely disagreed about how much excessive speculation drove energy price swings, so the bill's central premise was contested; overly tight position limits could push trading to genuinely offshore venues or reduce liquidity that hedgers rely on.
The bill relies on the CFTC to write and enforce detailed rules within fixed deadlines, and its effectiveness would depend entirely on an agency's willingness to police powerful traders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real and well-documented regulatory gap — trading in energy futures outside regulated exchanges — and the cost of closing it falls on large traders, not households. The honest objection is empirical: whether speculation was inflating energy prices was debated, and the bill's benefit to consumers depends on that premise. On balance, transparency and anti-manipulation tools at the CFTC are a modest cost for a meaningful check on a market every household pays into.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Agriculture Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, never receiving a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch introduced the Close the Enron Loophole Act on November 1, 2007, joined by Rep. Robert Andrews [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture, which holds jurisdiction over the Commodity Exchange Act and the CFTC [S1][S5].
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009 [S5].
The bill gathered 15 cosponsors, 12 Democrats and 3 Republicans, but bipartisan sponsorship never translated into committee action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Unregulated energy speculators and the electronic trading venues they use were better off: they kept operating without CFTC registration, position limits, or public price reporting for the rest of the Congress. Consumers continued bearing whatever effect unregulated speculation had on gasoline, heating oil, and natural gas prices.

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to close the Enron loophole and bring off-exchange energy trading under CFTC oversight [S1][S5].

for.name: Rep. Robert Andrews
for.what_they_did: Joined Welch in introducing the bill [S3].

against.name: Rep. Collin Peterson
against.what_they_did: His committee received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress [S5].

against.name: Energy derivatives exchanges and large energy traders
against.role: Operators of and traders on the off-exchange energy markets the bill targeted
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending CFTC registration, position limits, and reporting to off-exchange energy trading venues during the broader Enron loophole debate.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship leaned Democratic — 12 of the 15 cosponsors were Democrats, with 3 Republicans — and the Democratic chairman of the Agriculture Committee never moved the bill.

industries.industry: Off-exchange energy derivatives traders (speculators, hedge funds, banks)
industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful to trade energy futures on unregistered electronic facilities and subjects traders to position limits, forced liquidation of oversized positions, and five-year recordkeeping available to the CFTC and DOJ. Traders who profited from unregulated positions bear the cost; the mechanism the bill targets is price distortion in commodities every household buys [S3].

industries.industry: Electronic energy exchanges (e.g., ICE-style trading facilities)
industries.note: The bill strips these facilities of their exemption but offers a registration pathway with CFTC oversight, locking them in as the permanent registered venues for off-exchange energy trading. They lose their regulatory-free status but gain a legalized, codified role [S2][S3].

The bill requires the CFTC to keep position limits on off-exchange facilities at parity with those on regulated exchanges, ending a structure that let speculators avoid exchange limits. This removes a competitive disadvantage for compliant exchanges and hedgers [S2][S3].
